summary: Provides an overview of the attribute types and object classes defined by ISO and ITU-T in the X.500 documents, especially those intended for directory clients, for use with LDAPv3. It was replaced by several later RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a catalog of standard kinds of information, like name and address, that a directory entry can hold.

subtitle: A catalog of the standard X.500 attribute types and object classes, written out for LDAPv3 directories.

tldr.problem: LDAPv3 directories need an agreed set of attribute types and object classes so that clients and servers describe people, organizations and devices the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes the user-facing part of the X.500(96) schema: 55 attribute types, 7 syntaxes, 22 object classes and one matching rule, each written in LDAP's description format with its object identifier.
tldr.outcome: It was obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517, RFC 4519 and RFC 4523, and was updated by RFC 3377 before that.

today: RFC 2256 is obsolete. It was updated by RFC 3377 and replaced by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517, RFC 4519 and RFC 4523.

sections.title: What the Schema Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2256 gives an overview of the attribute types and object classes that the ISO and ITU-T committees defined in the X.500 documents, especially those meant for directory clients. The author calls it the most widely used schema for LDAP/X.500 directories, and says many other schema definitions for white pages objects use it as a basis.

It does not cover attributes used to administer X.500 directory servers, nor attributes defined by other ISO/ITU-T documents. The definitions come from X.501, X.520, X.509, X.521 and RFC 1274, and the memo says no new attribute definitions were added. Three attributes (supportedAlgorithms, deltaRevocationList and dmdName) and the dmd object class are new in the X.500(96) documents. Every definition is written in the format given in RFC 2252.

An IESG note warns that update access needs secure authentication that the document does not mandate. Implementors are discouraged from deploying LDAPv3 update functionality until a mandatory authentication standard is published.
sections.plainLanguage: Long ago, groups of experts made a standard list of what a directory entry can say about someone. This memo copies that list into a form the internet's directory system can use.

sections.title: Attribute Types
sections.content:
An LDAP server SHOULD recognize the attribute types in this section. Each entry gives a short description and a formal definition with an object identifier. Examples: cn (common name, typically a person's full name), sn (surname), c (a two-letter ISO 3166 country code), o (organization), ou (organizational unit), telephoneNumber and postalAddress.

Some attributes inherit from others. name is a supertype from which naming strings such as cn, sn and givenName are formed, and distinguishedName is the base for attributes like member and owner. Servers that lack attribute subtyping need not recognize these supertypes, and clients MUST NOT assume servers can do subtyping.

Certificate-related attributes such as userCertificate and cACertificate are stored and requested in binary form, for example as userCertificate;binary. A few are marked obsolete or unused: knowledgeInformation is no longer used, and searchGuide is obsoleted by enhancedSearchGuide.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute is one labeled box on a form, like "surname" or "phone number". Some boxes are cousins that share rules with a parent box.

sections.title: Syntaxes and Matching
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD recognize the syntaxes defined here. A syntax says how a value is written down. This RFC defines Delivery Method, Enhanced Guide, Guide, Octet String, Teletex Terminal Identifier, Telex Number and Supported Algorithm, mostly with a small BNF grammar and an example.

For instance, a Delivery Method value is one or more of words such as any, mhs, telephone and g3fax, joined by $. An Enhanced Guide value looks like person#(sn)#oneLevel. The Guide syntax should not be used for defining new attributes.

Section 8 lists one matching rule, octetStringMatch, and says servers MAY implement additional ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A syntax is the spelling rule for a box, such as "write the delivery method as one of these words". A matching rule says how to tell whether two answers are the same.

sections.title: Object Classes
sections.content:
An object class lists which attributes an entry MUST have and which it MAY have. Servers MUST recognize the classes top and subschema and SHOULD recognize the rest.

The classes include country, locality, organization, organizationalUnit, person, organizationalPerson, organizationalRole, groupOfNames, residentialPerson, device and dmd. For example, person must have sn and cn, and may have userPassword, telephoneNumber, seeAlso and description. organizationalPerson is a subclass of person that adds items such as title and ou.

Classes are STRUCTURAL or AUXILIARY. Auxiliary ones such as strongAuthenticationUser and certificationAuthority add certificate attributes to an entry.
sections.plainLanguage: An object class is a form template. The "person" form says you must write a surname and a name, and you may add a phone number if you like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The attributes describe real-world people, organizations and devices, and the RFC notes that most countries have privacy laws about publishing information on people.

Passwords in userPassword are stored as an octet string and are not encrypted. Sending cleartext passwords is strongly discouraged where the transport cannot guarantee confidentiality, because the password may be disclosed to unauthorized parties.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory holds facts about real people, so be careful who can see them. Never shout a password across a room where others can hear.

viz.caption: TWO DEFINITIONS COPIED FROM THE RFC

data.title: An attribute type and an object class
data.code:
( 2.5.4.3 NAME 'cn' SUP name )

( 2.5.6.6 NAME 'person' SUP top STRUCTURAL MUST ( sn $ cn )
  MAY ( userPassword $ telephoneNumber $ seeAlso $ description ) )
